title: Shloka 75
subtitle: Greater than everything, and living in a particular range of hills

namas.translation: Set her beside the whole universe and there is still something of her left over.

children.gloss: surpassing, more than, in excess of

namas.translation: What the Vedas are for is to make her knowable; strip that away and they say nothing.

compound.gloss: to be known by means of the Vedas

namas.translation: She has her seat in the Vindhya range, the wall of hills that divides the north of the land from the south.

compound.gloss: she who dwells on the Vindhya mountain

namas.translation: She arranges how things will fall out, doing for the world what Brahmā is credited with doing.

morphology.note: Feminine of the agent noun vidhātṛ, 'disposer, creator'.

namas.translation: The Vedas are born from her, not she from them.

compound.gloss: she who gives birth to the Vedas

children.gloss: mother, she who brings to birth

namas.translation: She is the power by which Viṣṇu throws the world up as an appearance and keeps it convincing.

compound.gloss: the illusory power belonging to Viṣṇu

children.gloss: creative illusion, the power of appearance

namas.translation: She moves for the pleasure of moving, and the shimmer of that play is what we see as the world.

commentary.meaning: Seven names on v, and the verse keeps changing the scale on which it is speaking. It opens as large as language allows — set her beside the universe and there is something left over — and follows that with a claim about how she is known: through the Veda. Then, without warning, an address. She lives in the Vindhya hills. The second line goes back up: she is the one who arranges how things will fall out, the Vedas are born from her, she is the power by which Viṣṇu holds the world together as an appearance, and she is play itself. The two Veda names are the hinge. If she is knowable through the Veda and the Veda is born from her, then the only road to her is one she built, and the verse says both things four names apart without appearing to notice a difficulty. Between them it puts her on a specific mountain, which is the sort of thing this hymn does when it is at its most confident.
commentary.history:
Viśvādhikā is a comparative built with an ablative: greater than the universe, exceeding it. The Puruṣa Sūkta had made the same claim by arithmetic — all beings are one quarter of him and three quarters stand immortal beyond — and the point of such formulations is to block the inference that if the divine is everything then it is exhausted by everything. The name is doing philosophical work in four syllables, and the work is the ordinary work of Vedānta, which is a good reminder that this hymn's tantric material sits inside a Vedāntic frame rather than beside it.

The two Veda names are best read as a pair even though three names separate them. Vedavedyā, to be known by means of the Vedas, is what a defender of the tradition's orthodoxy would want to say; the Gītā says it of Kṛṣṇa in almost the same words. Vedajananī, mother of the Vedas, reverses the dependency. Śrīvidyā spent much of its literary energy on exactly this manoeuvre, arguing that its mantra and its goddess were not extraneous to the Veda but its source and its secret meaning, and that a brahmin could therefore practise both without contradiction. The two names are that argument in miniature, and their placement on either side of a mountain address is a fair picture of how the text works: doctrine, geography, doctrine.

The Vindhyas are not a symbol. They are the range that runs east to west across the middle of the subcontinent and that Sanskrit geography treats as the boundary between the north and the south — a frontier, in older literature a place of forests and of peoples outside brahminical order. The goddess of that range, Vindhyavāsinī, has a temple at Vindhyachal near Mirzapur on the Ganges which is still one of the busiest goddess shrines in north India, and she was a major independent deity long before this hymn. The Devī Māhātmya records her at the moment of absorption: in the last chapter the goddess predicts her own future arrivals and says she will be born in the cowherd Nanda's house from Yaśodā's womb and, dwelling on the Vindhya mountain, destroy the demons. That verse is doing two things at once — attaching the Vindhya goddess to the Kṛṣṇa story, in which the infant girl exchanged for Kṛṣṇa escapes Kaṃsa's hands and takes to the hills, and attaching her to the great goddess. When the sahasranāma gives Lalitā the name, the absorption is complete and no longer needs explaining.

Viṣṇumāyā is the fourth name in this batch that hands her another deity's property. The Devī Māhātmya has a long litany in which the goddess is saluted under the name of whatever she is in all beings, and viṣṇumāyā heads the list. Behind the name is the story from that text's first chapter, in which the sleep that holds Viṣṇu is a goddess, and she must withdraw before he can wake and act. Read that way the compound is not saying she belongs to Viṣṇu; it is saying that the power everyone calls Viṣṇu's is a person, that she has her own name, and that Viṣṇu is at her disposal rather than the other way round.

Vilāsinī closes the verse with the tradition's favourite word for what the world is. The dictionary's sense for the noun is a lively, charming, coquettish woman, but vilāsa in this literature is a technical term: the shining-out or sporting of consciousness, manifestation undertaken for no reason except that it is in her nature to manifest. It is the word in the title of the Kāmakalāvilāsa, the treatise behind the second name of verse 73, where it names the unfolding of the point into a world. Placed at the end of a verse that has just called her greater than the universe, the ordainer, and the māyā of Viṣṇu, it defuses all three. What looks from below like arrangement, illusion and immensity is, from her side, play.
commentary.practice:
Seven names, all beginning with v, and the caesura falls after vedavedyā and after vedajananī. That leaves the two longest names, vindhyācalanivāsinī and the pair viṣṇumāyā vilāsinī, filling the second half of each line.

The great gift of this verse is that it puts all three Sanskrit sibilants in it, and the contrast is easy to hear once pointed out. Viśvādhikā has ś, the palatal, made with the tongue against the hard palate — the nearest English sound is the sh of "sheep", said with the tongue flat and forward. Viṣṇumāyā has ṣ, the retroflex, made with the tongue-tip curled well back, a duller and darker sound. Vilāsinī has plain dental s, the tip at the teeth. Say viśva, viṣṇu, vilāsinī in a row, three times, and this verse will have taught you the distinction that the whole stotra depends on.

Vindhyācalanivāsinī opens with a three-consonant cluster, न्ध्य: n, then the aspirated dh, then y. All three are dental or palatal and close together, so the sequence is fast rather than difficult, but the aspiration must be audible — vindhya, not vindya. The same aspirated dh returns immediately in vidhātrī, where it is followed by the cluster tr, so the second line begins with two clusters in five syllables: vi-dhā-trī.

Viśvādhikā contains a sandhi worth reconstructing: viśva plus adhikā, two short a sounds merged into one long ā, giving viśvādhikā and hiding the word-boundary completely. This is the commonest vowel sandhi in the language and the one that most often defeats a beginner trying to look a name up in a dictionary. Split it before you search.

Viṣṇumāyā has the cluster ṣṇ, retroflex sibilant into retroflex nasal — the tongue curls back for the ṣ and stays exactly where it is for the ṇ, with no movement between them. This is the same economy you met in aṣṭamī in verse 5 and will meet again in the ṣ names of verse 84. Keep the u short: viṣ-ṇu, not viṣ-ṇū.

Watch the ordinary vowels too. Vedavedyā has four short e and a sounds and one long ā, and the dy in the middle is dental d into y. Vedajananī is five short vowels and a long ī at the end, the lightest name in the verse; vidhātrī, immediately before it, is two longs and nothing else. Alternating those two correctly is what gives the second line its shape.

On what to hold while chanting: the verse is an exercise in refusing to choose between the vast and the local. It is easy to chant the abstractions with attention and let the mountain go past as a piece of geography, and that is the wrong way round. The tradition's claim is not that she is everywhere in general. It is that she is everywhere and also in the Vindhyas in particular, where there is a temple with a queue outside it, and that neither statement weakens the other. Ten verses further on the hymn will name two more places by name, and this is where it starts.

crossReferences.translation: So great is his greatness — and the Puruṣa is greater still than that. All beings are one quarter of him; three quarters of him are the deathless in heaven.
crossReferences.relevance: The oldest form of the claim that viśvādhikā compresses into four syllables. The arithmetic is the argument: if the whole visible world is a fraction, then exhausting the world does not exhaust the source. Every later formulation of divine transcendence in this literature, including this one, is working with the fraction the hymn set.

crossReferences.translation: I am seated in the heart of everyone; memory, knowledge and their loss come from me. I alone am what is to be known by all the Vedas; I am the maker of the Veda's end and the knower of the Veda too.
crossReferences.relevance: Vedavedyā is this line turned into a name and given to her. Notice that the Gītā verse also claims both halves of the circle at once — to be what the Vedas know and to be the author of their conclusion — so the apparent circularity in this verse is a standard move rather than a slip. What is distinctive in the stotra is only that the two halves are stated as separate names.

crossReferences.iast: nandagopagṛhe jātā yaśodāgarbhasambhavā | tatas tau nāśayiṣyāmi vindhyācalanivāsinī ||
crossReferences.translation: Born in the house of Nanda the cowherd, sprung from Yaśodā's womb, I shall then destroy those two — I, who dwell on the Vindhya mountain.
crossReferences.relevance: The name in this verse is a whole verse in the older text, and it appears there at the moment of annexation: the goddess is listing the forms in which she will return, and the Vindhya goddess is one of them. The Kṛṣṇa connection is part of the same operation. By the time the sahasranāma uses vindhyācalanivāsinī as a simple epithet, the local deity of a north Indian hill shrine has become an attribute of the supreme.

crossReferences.deva: या देवी सर्वभूतेषु विष्णुमायेति शब्दिता । नमस्तस्यै नमस्तस्यै नमस्तस्यै नमो नमः ॥
crossReferences.iast: yā devī sarvabhūteṣu viṣṇumāyeti śabditā | namas tasyai namas tasyai namas tasyai namo namaḥ ||
crossReferences.translation: The goddess who in all beings is called by the name Viṣṇu's māyā — to her salutation, to her salutation, to her salutation, salutation and salutation again.
crossReferences.relevance: The opening verse of the most-chanted litany in the older goddess text, and the source of this name's authority. The formula matters as much as the content: what follows in that hymn is a long series of the same shape, in which consciousness, intelligence, sleep, hunger, shadow, power, thirst, patience and error are each in turn saluted as her. Viṣṇumāyā heads the list, which is where the sahasranāma found it.

references.title: India: A Sacred Geography
references.author: Diana L. Eck (Harmony Books, 2012)
references.note: For why a mountain range belongs in a list of metaphysical attributes. Eck's subject is precisely the habit of mind that puts the supreme in a named place without thinking it has thereby limited her, and the chapters on the goddess's landscape are the best preparation for the pīṭha names eight verses ahead.
